# Anthropic says its AI models hacked 3 organizations during testing

By 

CHAN HO-HIM
, 
AP Business Writer

Updated

Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing, just days after ChatGPT maker OpenAI raised concerns over AI control after it disclosed its rogue models hacked another company.

Anthropic, the San Francisco-based AI company behind Claude, posted on its website Thursday that it discovered the three incidents after reviewing more than 141,000 evaluation runs. [...] Last week, OpenAI said its AI models went rogue during an evaluation of its models, and broke into the servers of AI startup Hugging Face. OpenAI described it as a “significant security incident.”

These incidents have highlighted the vulnerabilities in AI security and control and raised questions over how AI can be safely under human control as the technology’s usage becomes more widespread globally.

“Safety testing happens before a model is released precisely because we don’t yet know what it is capable of,” Anthropic said on Thursday on its website.

items.content:
In January, researchers at the Army Engineering University published a paper on the threat of “data-free distillation,” a method of reverse-engineering a model’s capabilities without direct access to its core parameters.

To counter that vulnerability, they proposed defense mechanisms designed to mask the hidden logical information exposed in a model’s public outputs.

Distilled models also inherit only selected capabilities and cannot fully replicate the broad intelligence of frontier systems.

Trevor Koverko, co-founder of AI data company Sapien, said distilled models remain less capable than their teacher models.

“It is best understood as transferring selected capabilities into a cheaper, locally controlled system, not achieving independence from frontier AI.”

###### Share: [...] A 2024 paper from the PLA’s National University of Defense Technology described using distillation to shrink an image-processing model for deployment on unmanned aerial vehicles, allowing drones to analyse live video and support navigation and targeting decisions in real time even when communications are cut.

Similarly, researchers at China’s Academy of Military Sciences used distillation to run a target-recognition model on tactical hardware during simulated maritime operations involving drones, ships and unmanned submarines, a study published earlier this year showed.

#### BENEFITS AND LIMITS [...] Sunny Cheung, a Jamestown fellow who analysed over 60 of the papers, said Chinese military scientists are systematically capturing the reasoning steps of Western models to adapt them for surveillance, cyber warfare and tactical decision-making.

“Teaching a model the right answer is one thing but teaching it the reasoning behind the answer is much harder,” said Cheung.

“These papers show Chinese military-linked researchers are trying to transfer that expensive, proprietary reasoning from Western models into smaller systems they can control and deploy locally.”

## The role of BCI in music

The same alignment approach was demonstrated in the co-authored paper R&B – rhythm and brain: Cross subject decoding of music from human brain activity, accepted at Neural Networks. In this study, researchers recorded brain scans (fMRI) from five people as they listened to 540 songs spanning 10 genres, then built a model that translates neural activity into an AI representation of the music itself.

Using a technique that aligns brain patterns across different people’s brains, the model could identify the correct genre being heard about 61% of the time (versus 10% by chance), and pinpoint the exact song among 60 candidates roughly 25% of the time (versus under 2% by chance), setting a new benchmark for this task. [...] Until now, these systems had to be built separately for each patient, since every brain’s signals are different. The paper proposes the first cross-subject neural-to-phoneme decoding model trained on invasive recordings from multiple participants implanted in distinct cortical regions.

Rather than treating each participant as an isolated case, Tether’s approach leverages shared speech patterns. It uses this shared understanding to train one decoder that can then be quickly adjusted for each new patient. [...] Although every brain is different, and across different people representations of speech can vary (due to different implantation location, different functional activity, and different learning curricula), researchers have been able to show that a single model, trained with the right alignment technique, can generalise across people rather than being rebuilt for each one.

That leaves companies without evidence that the same protections work for users who speak other languages. Connecting an AI model to other software raises the consequences of failure. An AI agent—a system that can take actions through other software—may send email, move money or change records, causing a manipulated instruction or unsafe output to trigger a real action. “A chatbot’s worst case is a bad answer. But an agent’s worst case is a bad action,” Schwartz said. Agents also read emails, web pages, documents and information returned by other tools. Any of that content can contain text the system interprets as a command, and one manipulated step can influence the next. “Anything it reads can carry instructions. The content becomes the attacker,” he [...] “A guardrail that was tested once, in one language, against polite users is like a seatbelt made of paper,” he said.

AI guardrails, the filters and rules meant to block unsafe prompts and responses, need to reflect what the system is built to do. A legal or medical assistant may need to handle sensitive requests that a general chatbot would restrict. An internal banking tool may be allowed to discuss financial matters that a public chatbot should avoid. The controls should check both what users ask and what the AI returns.
